mcqs.question: Brute-force search on text = "aaaaaaaaab" with pattern = "aaab" repeatedly matches 3 characters before failing on the 4th. What does brute force do with that partial-match information?
options: It stores it in a lookup table for the next starting position to reuse
It discards it entirely and restarts the comparison from scratch at the next position
It uses it to skip ahead by the length of the partial match
It uses it to shrink the pattern for future comparisons
mcqs.explanation: Brute force's inner loop always starts j back at 0 for the next starting position, throwing away every character of progress from the previous attempt. That's exactly the inefficiency KMP's LPS array is built to eliminate by reusing that information instead.

mcqs.question: For pattern = "ababaca", what does lps[3] (looking at the substring "abab") represent, and what is its value?
options: The number of times "a" appears in "abab", which is 2
The index of the first repeated character in "abab", which is 1
The length of the longest proper prefix of "abab" that is also a proper suffix of it, which is 2
The length of "abab" itself, which is 4
mcqs.explanation: lps[i] is defined as the length of the longest proper prefix of pattern[0..i] that's also a proper suffix of that same substring — for "abab" that's "ab", length 2, since "ab" opens and closes it and no longer match exists. It has nothing to do with character counts or the substring's own length.

mcqs.question: During KMP's main scan, what happens to the text pointer i when a mismatch occurs partway through a match?
options: It stays fixed while j jumps back using the LPS array — i never moves backward
It moves back to the position where the current match attempt began
It resets to 0 and the scan restarts from the beginning of the text
It advances by the length of the pattern regardless of how much matched
mcqs.explanation: KMP's core invariant is that i only ever moves forward — on a mismatch, only j falls back via lps[j-1], and the comparison retries at the same text position. That invariant is exactly what bounds the total work on the text to O(n) rather than re-scanning characters per restart.

mcqs.question: In the main KMP scan, after matching j characters and then hitting a mismatch, which value should the pattern pointer fall back to?
options: 0, since any mismatch means starting the pattern over is always correct
lps[j] — the LPS value at the current position
lps[j - 1] — the LPS value of the last character that was actually matched
j - 1, decrementing by exactly one regardless of the pattern's structure
mcqs.explanation: The fallback uses lps[j - 1], the LPS value of the last matched character, because that's the longest prefix-that's-also-a-suffix guaranteed to already be sitting in the text at this point. Using lps[j] is the classic off-by-one that silently produces wrong matches without crashing.

mcqs.question: You're scanning untrusted, adversary-controlled network payloads for a fixed signature pattern. Why would you specifically want KMP's guarantee over brute force here?
options: KMP uses less memory than brute force in every case
Brute force cannot handle patterns longer than a few characters
KMP is easier to implement correctly than brute force
An adversary who controls the input can construct text that triggers brute force's O(n·m) worst case on purpose, while KMP's O(n+m) bound holds regardless of input shape
mcqs.explanation: Brute force's worst case isn't just theoretical — an adversary who shapes the input can deliberately trigger it, turning a linear-feeling scan into a quadratic one. KMP's bound holds no matter what the input looks like, which is exactly the guarantee you want against adversarial data; it uses slightly more memory (the LPS array) and is not simpler to implement, so neither of those is the reason.

mcqs.question: While building the LPS array, a character mismatch occurs and the current running length is greater than 0. What does build_lps do next?
options: It resets length to 0 immediately and moves to the next index
It sets lps[i] to -1 to mark the mismatch
It skips that index entirely and leaves lps[i] undefined
It sets length to lps[length - 1] and retries the comparison, rather than resetting length to 0
mcqs.explanation: The self-referential fallback — length = lps[length - 1] — is what keeps LPS construction O(m); resetting to 0 on every mismatch would throw away information the array itself already encodes and can degrade to O(m^2) on repetitive patterns. Every index of lps is always assigned some value, never left undefined or negative.
